source.title: Generalizability of Memorization Neural Networks
source.authors: Li-Jia Yu; Xiao-Shan Gao; Li-Jun Zhang; Yi-Bo Miao

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, including appendices and experiment tables.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes theoretical and algorithmic memorization, but does not test the listed versions’ conditions: standard gradient training, random-label fitting, width sweeps, optimizer or batch changes, dropout, sharpness, or removal of memorized examples.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical results and test-set accuracies for networks constructed by its own memorization algorithm, plus an SGD-trained comparator. These do not test the listed versions’ specified methods or conditions. Cited prior-work claims are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study proves properties of constructed interpolating networks and evaluates their natural-label accuracy. It does not compare the same architecture and training recipe on random versus natural labels (V1), measure test error while widening beyond interpolation (V2), or perform the comparisons named in V3–V8. Its deliberately poor-generalizing construction is not evidence against those versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors establish structural restrictions and sample-complexity results for constructive memorization algorithms, show that some interpolating constructions generalize poorly despite ample i.i.d. data, and give a polynomial-time construction with a conditional generalization guarantee. They acknowledge that its CIFAR-10 test accuracy falls below SGD-trained networks and emphasize its theoretical purpose.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies constructive memorization algorithms and theoretical guarantees, with a separate SGD-trained ResNet18 comparator; it does not reproduce the listed original methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different empirical outcomes across binary label pairs, including weaker memorization-algorithm accuracy for some CIFAR-10 pairs.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 5.3 constructs an interpolating network with population accuracy at most 0.51 under positive separation and bounded density, deliberately arranging poor predictions outside the training set.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perfect interpolation alone does not guarantee generalization; a construction can fit every training label while generalizing poorly.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 7.3 guarantees population accuracy at least 1−ε with probability at least 1−δ when N≥SD ln(SD/δ)/ε. Its constructed networks obtain 0.91–0.99 accuracy on binary MNIST tasks and 0.54–0.87 on binary CIFAR-10 tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A particular polynomial-time interpolation construction can generalize under separation and sample-coverage conditions, with empirical performance depending on the task.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet18 trained for 20 epochs achieves 0.96–0.99 test accuracy on the binary CIFAR-10 tasks, exceeding the construction's corresponding results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ordinary ResNet18 training outperforms this constructive memorization algorithm on the tested binary CIFAR-10 tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 5.1 establishes that for every fixed width w there exists a positively separated distribution in dimension n>w on which networks restricted to that width have accuracy at most 0.51.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A fixed-width architecture cannot guarantee generalization uniformly over positively separated distributions of arbitrarily higher dimension.

record.peer_reviewed: 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024)
record.problems: The empirical result tables report pair-specific accuracies but the text does not give uncertainty estimates. The paper’s memorization algorithm is a constructed procedure, so its results do not establish outcomes for standard gradient training on random labels.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1–4 contain separate accuracies for individual label pairs and memorization methods. Those pair-level values were not extracted; the text supplies aggregate descriptions for Tables 1–3, and Table 4 compares alternative memorization constructions rather than a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Fitting fixed random labels and comparing held-out performance on random and natural labels using the same architecture and training recipe.
The trajectory of test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks trained from scratch with gradient methods, including local connectivity and initialization effects.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, weight decay changes, or optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and changes to the training recipe.
Dropout effects, including training-set size, underfitting, augmentation, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps relative to other measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Here memorization means exact interpolation, rather than the example-inclusion influence measure used in V8. Neither the width necessity theorem nor comparisons between interpolation constructions establish V2's post-interpolation width trend. No verdict labels are warranted for V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label condition or comparison of the same architecture and recipe on random versus natural labels; the paper’s constructed memorization algorithm is not standard gradient training.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks trained from scratch.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.

rows.subject: memorization network F for Dtr
rows.stage_stated: constructed by the algorithm in Theorem 5.3
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 5.3 gives an upper bound on distribution accuracy for a memorization network under the stated density and separation assumptions.
rows.note: The theorem asserts existence of a memorization network with this accuracy bound; it is not a standard-gradient training result.
rows.check: The parameter bound drops a square root: Theorem 5.3 states O(n + sqrt(N) ln(Nnr/c)). This is an existence theorem for a construction deliberately designed to misclassify unseen points, not an observed failure of a listed claim. The accuracy bound ≤0.51 is correctly recorded.

rows.subject: memorization network Fmem
rows.stage_stated: constructed by the algorithm in Theorem 7.3
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 7.3 gives a high-probability distribution-accuracy guarantee for the constructed memorization network.
rows.note: This is a theoretical guarantee for the paper’s own algorithm.
rows.check: The probability guarantee and sample-size condition are correctly recorded, but they concern the paper's constructive algorithm under positive class separation; they do not measure any listed version.

rows.value: Individual pair accuracies are reported in Table 3
rows.locator: Appendix I.2, Table 3 and accompanying text
rows.note: The paper states that the normal-training results are significantly better than Table 2; the table gives separate values for each label pair.
rows.check: This is the paper's method-versus-training comparator, not a listed-claim result. Table 3 reports actual test accuracies of 0.96–0.99, rather than the recorded placeholder. Comparing trained ResNet18 with a constructed network does not test V3's comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks both trained from scratch with gradient methods. 'Significantly better' is the authors' description; no statistical significance analysis is supplied.
